objectives.q: Can people who are new to GitHub find what they came for, without help?
objectives.how: Usability tests with the five commonest tasks; time, success and where people hesitate.

objectives.q: Which questions bring people to the catalogue, and which views answer them?
objectives.how: Interviews and the survey; compare with the role-based questions on Home.

objectives.q: Do people understand and trust the evidence labels, such as 'part of a live service', and their measured accuracy?
objectives.how: Usability tests: ask people to explain a label in their own words, and whether they'd act on it.

objectives.q: What stops people who use assistive technology from using the catalogue?
objectives.how: Sessions with screen reader, magnification, voice and switch users; fixes go straight into the backlog.

objectives.q: Which handovers to the DAM capability playbooks and the DQ Commons help, and which confuse?
objectives.how: Cross-portal journey tests (the six journeys in the three-portal review).

objectives.q: Who needs this catalogue to keep existing, and who should own and fund it?
objectives.how: Interviews with data leaders, architects and policy leads; the owner's decision on a home (roadmap RM-11).

objectives.q: Should it become a registered govukOS node and a source of data feeds for other services?
objectives.how: Interviews with the teams behind GTI, ANA, LIAH and the shared registers; test the data/xref.json feed.

objectives.q: How does it serve the government's strategy for data, including the forthcoming Strategic Data Roadmap?
objectives.how: Map findings to the roadmap for modern digital government; re-map when the Strategic Data Roadmap is published.

objectives.q: How fresh and complete does the data need to be for people to rely on it?
objectives.how: Survey and interviews; compare with what refreshing costs (roadmap RM-09 and RM-10).

objectives.q: Is the split between the open edition and the government edition right?
objectives.how: Interviews with government and public sector users, and with people outside government.

methods.name: Conversation about your work
methods.who: Anyone who might use the catalogue
methods.what: We ask about your work, how you find out what others in government have built, and what gets in the way. No preparation needed.

methods.name: Try the catalogue
methods.mode: Online, one to one, sharing your screen
methods.who: Anyone, especially people new to GitHub
methods.what: You try four or five everyday tasks while thinking aloud. We're testing the catalogue, not you.

methods.name: Accessibility session
methods.mode: Online or in person, with your own set-up
methods.who: People who use a screen reader, magnification, voice control, a switch or other assistive technology
methods.what: You use the catalogue with your own set-up and tell us what works and what gets in the way. We pay for interpreters and support.

methods.name: Five-minute survey
methods.mode: A GitHub form, in your own time
methods.what: Seven questions about what you use the catalogue for and what's missing. Only totals are published, and counts under 5 are hidden.

methods.name: Journey across three portals
methods.who: Data leaders, stewards, architects, service owners
methods.what: You follow a task that starts in one of the DAM playbooks, the DQ Commons or this catalogue and carries on in another.

methods.name: Ideas and votes
methods.what: Suggest an idea, or add a thumbs-up to the ideas you want most. Votes help us decide what to do next.

quotas: Devolved government or public body in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland
NHS or other health and care body
Outside government: supplier, academic or civil society
People who have never used GitHub
People working outside London and the South East
inclusion: Sessions at different times of day, with breaks, and a phone option.
Captions on video calls; a British Sign Language interpreter on request, paid for from the research budget.
Materials sent in advance, in large print, easy read or Welsh on request.
Your own device and set-up for accessibility sessions; we never ask you to install anything.
Age, sex, ethnicity and disability are asked only if you choose to answer, and reported only as totals, never against a person.

tasks.text: Your minister has asked whether any public body has built a tool for checking addresses. Find out, and who to ask.
Find out what your organisation publishes as code that is about data quality or catalogues.
You're building a form for a new service. Find a component others in government already use for this.
Find which of your organisation's projects may rely on technology that is no longer supported.
Find which organisations use the DCAT standard in their code, and how you'd link to that list from another site.
Something in a project's description is wrong. Tell the maintainers.

criteria.name: Value to users
criteria.how: 3: research shows it blocks people, or it has 10 or more votes. 2: it slows people down, or 5 to 9 votes. 1: a nice-to-have. 0: no evidence yet.

criteria.name: Reach
criteria.how: How many of the six personas it helps: 1 for one, 2 for two or three, 3 for four or more.

criteria.name: Strategic fit
criteria.how: How directly it serves the themes above: 3 directly, 2 indirectly, 1 slightly, 0 not at all.

criteria.name: Feasibility
criteria.how: 3: small, no dependencies. 2: medium, or needs one other team. 1: large, or needs a decision by the owner. 0: not possible now.

capacity: Capacity is a gate, not a score. Each quarter the maintainers say how many points of work they can take on; items go into Now in score order until it's full, then Next. Anything needing the owner's decision waits for it, however high it scores.

backlog.title: Test the catalogue with 5 to 8 people from at least four audiences who don't use GitHub
backlog.why: Nothing has been tested with users yet; this research bundle starts it. Needs facilitators and participants.

backlog.title: Re-read GitHub so projects found since the catalogue was built are added
backlog.why: Fresh data is what people will rely on (objective S4); each refresh needs a person.

backlog.title: A named team accepts ownership: answers issues, reviews pull requests and reviews the catalogue every quarter
backlog.why: Without a named owning team nothing else is sustainable (objective S1); the owner's decision.

backlog.title: Join projects to the datasets they publish or use in data catalogues (data.gov.uk, statistics.gov.scot, Data Map Wales, NHS catalogues)
backlog.why: Joining code to the datasets it publishes serves the data infrastructure theme directly; large, and needs the catalogues' data.

backlog.title: Check the catalogue manually with screen readers, magnifiers at 400% zoom and speech input
backlog.why: Manual accessibility testing is the gap automated checks can't close; needs a specialist.

backlog.title: Link repositories to the systems they belong to
backlog.why: Linking code to the systems it belongs to supports upgrading legacy systems; depends on LIAH.

backlog.title: Run the roadmap as a GitHub project board, with each item an issue
backlog.why: A board shows everyone the status of each item, in the open.

backlog.title: Ask organisations to check their profile and say whether the next steps are useful
backlog.why: Organisations confirming their own profile makes it trustworthy; needs them to take part.

backlog.title: Collect GitHub feature settings (Issues, Projects, Wiki, Discussions) for every project, not a sample
backlog.why: Feature settings for every project replace an estimate; needs a token and a person to run it.

backlog.title: Move the repository to its agreed home organisation
backlog.why: A permanent home keeps links stable; follows RM-12.

backlog.title: Create the labels the issue and discussion forms apply: contact, profile check, label check and roadmap
backlog.why: Labels make issues filterable and group release notes; minutes for the owner.

backlog.title: Create a Q&A category in Discussions, with the slug q-a
backlog.why: Questions Ask can't answer get a public, searchable answer.

backlog.title: Measure the precision of each topic on a labelled sample, as was done for strategy and DAM tags
backlog.why: Measured precision for topics, as for other labels; the label-check form already collects the sample.

backlog.title: Add boundaries and locations so nations, authorities and councils can be shown on maps
backlog.why: Maps help devolved and local users; needs boundary data and design work.

backlog.title: Require a person to approve each GitHub Pages deployment
backlog.why: A person approves every publish: the catalogue's own rule, enforced by GitHub.
